messages.content:
Hi genealogy enthusiasts! My brother and I both did DNA tests for fun over the holidays and just got our results back. We were comparing them tonight and some things seem really weird - can someone help us understand what we're looking at? We're both confused and wondering if maybe the lab made a mistake.

My Results:
- Irish/Scottish: 45%
- German: 23%
- Scandinavian: 18%
- Italian: 14%

My Brother's Results:
- Irish/Scottish: 46%
- German: 22%
- Eastern European: 31%
- Middle Eastern: 1%

Here's what's confusing us:

DNA Relatives section:
- We show up as "Close Family" to each other
- We share 1,847 cM (centimorgans) - not sure what this means?
- I match with cousins on "Mom's side": Karen, Susan, Michael (all 400-600 cM)
- He matches with the same cousins: Karen, Susan, Michael (same amounts)
- But on "Dad's side" it's weird:
    - I match with cousin Tommy (578 cM) and Uncle Jim's kids (390 cM each)
    - My brother shows NO matches to Tommy or Uncle Jim's kids at all
    - Instead he has matches to people with names I don't recognize

We're only 2 years apart and our parents have been married 30 years! We look so much alike that everyone says we could be twins. Is this normal? Maybe different kids inherit different sides of the family more strongly?

We were going to surprise Mom and Dad with a big family tree project for their anniversary next month. Should we contact the DNA company about what seems like missing connections?

It's great that you both got your DNA results and are diving into learning about your ancestry! The confusion is actually quite common, and there are a few things to consider:

1. DNA Inheritance: Everybody inherits a completely different combination of DNA from their parents. You and your brother both got 50% of your DNA from your mother, but you received a different half from your father than he did. That's why you will sometimes match with relatives that he doesn't, and vice versa. Sometimes specific ethnic populations can be carried for generations before showing up again in DNA results.

2. Ancestral Doubling: The Irish and Scottish heritage you and your brother share is likely the result of "ancestral doubling." This occurs when the same ancestors appear on both sides of your family tree, often through intermarriage and travel. This can make the results appear credibly large, even if the actual common ancestors are further back than it seems.

3. Cognatic Descent: This refers to descent through the female line. Since you inherited more DNA from your mother's side than your brother did, this could explain some of the differences you're seeing.

4. C-centimorgans (cM): The cM is a unit of genetic linkage disequilibrium. In other words, it bezeichnet the likelihood that a particular region of DNA that was recently inherited from ancestors will remain together as it gets passed down to future generations. The 1,847 cM you share means that the region of your DNA is very likely to come from parents/grandparents, making you siblings.

5. Ancestry Gap: Your dad's side seems missing in your brother's results. This is intriguingly bizarre but can happen. It's possible that he inherited more DNA from your mother's side, or that the regions on your father's side of the family's DNA are not well-represented in the database the kit used.

It seems like you don't need to contact the DNA company since these discrepancies are not unusual but rather build on the complexity of human genetics and family history. Congratulations on your newfound knowledge! Now you can start tracing your ancestors back. Good luck with your family tree project!
